title: Construct the Longest New String
statement:
You own `x` copies of the two-letter string `"AA"`, `y` copies of `"BB"` and `z` copies of `"AB"`. Pick any number of these pieces (from none to all of them), put them in any order, and join them end to end into a single string. The result is allowed only if it never has three equal letters in a row, that is, it contains neither `"AAA"` nor `"BBB"` anywhere.

Return the largest length an allowed string can have.
signature: int longestString(int x, int y, int z)
notes:
## Intuition

Look at which piece may follow which. After `"AA"` only `"BB"` fits, because any piece starting with `A` would create `"AAA"`. Before `"BB"` only `"AA"` fits (or nothing), because a piece ending in `B` would create `"BBB"`. So the `"AA"` and `"BB"` pieces must strictly alternate, and the more common kind can be used at most once more than the rarer kind.

The `"AB"` pieces never get in the way: a chain `"ABAB...AB"` is valid, it can sit at the very front of an alternating run that starts with `"AA"`, or right after a final `"BB"` (giving `"BBAB"`). So every `"AB"` is always used. A brute force could search every order of pieces, but this counting argument gives the answer directly.

## Approach

1. `pairs = min(x, y)`: that many `"AA"`/`"BB"` pairs always alternate safely, giving `2 * pairs` blocks.
2. If `x` and `y` differ, one extra block of the more common kind fits at an end of the run.
3. Add all `z` `"AB"` blocks.
4. Every block has two letters, so return `2 * blocks`.

## Example 1, step by step

`x = 2`, `y = 5`, `z = 1`.

- `pairs = min(2, 5) = 2`, so `blocks = 4`.
- `x !== y`, so one extra `"BB"` fits: `blocks = 5` (`BB AA BB AA BB`).
- Add the single `"AB"` at the end: `blocks = 6`, string `"BBAABBAABBAB"`.
- Return `2 * 6 = 12`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1), a few arithmetic operations.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Using every `"AA"` and `"BB"` is impossible when the counts differ by more than one; only one extra block of the larger kind fits.
- When `x === y` there is no extra block: `AA BB ... AA BB` already uses everything.
- `"AB"` pieces do not reduce how many `"AA"` or `"BB"` you can use, so do not subtract anything for them.
- The answer is a length in letters: multiply the number of pieces by 2.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pairs` | number of full `"AA"` + `"BB"` pairs, `min(x, y)` |
| `blocks` | number of two-letter pieces used in the best string |

narration.2: AA and BB must alternate, so the rarer kind limits how many complete AA/BB pairs fit.
narration.4: When the counts differ, there is a spare piece of the more common kind...
narration.5: ...and it fits at one end of the alternating run.
narration.7: Every AB can always be added at the front or after the last BB without breaking the rule.
narration.8: Each piece has two letters, so the length is twice the number of pieces.
